title: Life cycle close
hook: a life, from the adhan in the ear to the prayer without an adhan

segments.voice: Yesterday, inheritance, lived: dividing what someone leaves by the shares, with fairness and peace. Your line: shares with peace. Did a family come to mind where the peace mattered more than the split? Today, the whole road at once. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

A baby, a few hours old, in someone's arms. A parent or a grandparent leans in close to the tiny right ear and says the adhan, softly: Allahu akbar. Some families do this, and it's where this whole stretch of the path began. Now the other end of the road. A funeral. People stand in rows behind the imam for the funeral prayer, and before it, no adhan is called at all. No call. Just the prayer. Some people put those two moments side by side and say a life is the space between the call and the prayer. That's a saying people tell, not a verse. But it makes a good map for today, the last day of the life cycle.
screen: `THE CALL IN A NEWBORN'S EAR.` → `A PRAYER WITH NO CALL.` → `A LIFE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Walk the road again, quickly, and watch whose hands are doing the work. At the start: someone else says the call in your ear. Someone else touches a softened date to your mouth, chooses your name, shares the meat of the sacrifice, shaves your hair and gives its weight in silver. You do none of it. You're carried. Then the middle, and the hands become yours. Learning to pray. Finishing the Qur'an, the khatm. Coming of age, when the duties begin. Choosing a spouse, giving consent, the nikah, a home where, as surah al-Rum puts it, two people may dwell in tranquillity. Serving a family, shepherding a flock, honoring the elders who once carried you. Then the road bends again. Visiting the sick. Remembering death. And at the end, the hands go back to the community: someone washes you, wraps you in plain white cloth, stands in rows to pray over you, lays you facing the qiblah, cooks for your family, writes the shares of what you left. The Qur'an says it plainly in surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's words: "Every soul will taste of death." And it gives a line for the moment the news comes. Surah al-Baqarah describes the patient, who say when misfortune strikes: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Allah's at the start, returning at the end. So the shape of a Muslim life, as these customs draw it, is carried, then carrying, then carried again. The part in the middle is the part a person lives with their own hands. And that middle is where the next stretch of the path goes: the festival year, the days and months Muslims keep while they're still walking.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE SAYS YOUR CALL.` · `THE MIDDLE IS YOURS TO LIVE.` · `SOMEONE ELSE SAYS YOUR PRAYER.` · `CARRIED, CARRYING, CARRIED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: find your own stage on the road. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Ask, without hurrying: where am I right now? Being carried, by parents, by people caring for me? Carrying, with someone depending on my hands? Or somewhere in between? Notice who carried you to get here. Notice who you're carrying now, even in a small way. You don't need to judge the stage. Just know where you're standing. If you pray, you can remember the people at both ends of your road. The bell holds the time.
Life cycle close. The whole road, from the adhan in a newborn's ear to the funeral prayer that has no adhan, with the community's hands at both ends. Today's word.

Your line: from call to prayer. Today, the next time you hear a call to prayer, a bell, or an alarm, let it ask you one thing: what are my hands carrying right now? Tomorrow, the sacred months. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Some Muslim families say the adhan softly in a newborn's ear, and at the end of life the community washes, shrouds and prays over the body in a funeral prayer that has no adhan; on hearing of a death, the words of Qur'an 2:156 are said: "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning."

notes: Confirm the statement that no adhan or iqamah is called for the funeral prayer (the standard position across the schools).
The saying that a life is the space between the adhan at birth and the funeral prayer is presented as a saying people tell, not a source. Confirm the framing.
Abu Dawud 5105 on the adhan in the newborn's ear is graded weak by some hadith scholars; the script says only that some families do this.
The teach recaps the block's days (date, naming, sacrifice, hair, prayer, khatm, nikah, etc.) without numbers; confirm the recap matches the earlier scripts.
Confirm Pickthall's exact wording of 3:185 (first sentence) and 2:156.
Editor pass: howItsDone no longer says all Muslims say 2:156 on hearing of a death; the note on Abu Dawud 5105 now matches the script's 'some families'.
